selected.title: Could a tiny sample from Phobos explain how Mars got its moons?
selected.summary: Japan’s MMX spacecraft is scheduled to launch on October 20 JST, aiming to study Mars’s moons and return a Phobos sample to Earth. The mission could help test whether the moons formed from a Mars-impact event or were captured asteroids.
selected.why_it_matters: A sample could reshape ideas about how planetary systems form and inform future exploration of Mars and its moons.
selected.challenge_question: What is Japan’s MMX mission designed to bring back to Earth?
selected.answer_explanation: MMX is designed to collect a sample from Phobos, one of Mars’s moons, and return it to Earth. The spacecraft is scheduled to launch October 20 in Japan (October 19 UTC); this is a mission plan, not a completed sample return.
selected.butterfly_question: If Phobos formed from a huge impact on Mars, what might its sample reveal about the early planet—and the conditions that made life possible?

selected.title: Parents say babies matter—but do they think help is worth the cost?
selected.summary: A University of Michigan national poll reports that 81% of parents say having a baby is more expensive than it should be, while 59% say supporting families with young children is a good use of taxpayer dollars.
selected.why_it_matters: The contrast highlights a real-world tension between household financial pressure and public support for early-childhood programs.
selected.challenge_question: In a University of Michigan poll, what share said having a baby is too expensive?
selected.answer_explanation: The poll found that 81% of surveyed parents agreed having a baby is more expensive than it should be—roughly four in five. It also found lower agreement, 59%, that supporting families with young children is a good use of taxpayer dollars.
selected.butterfly_question: If families need early support but public backing is mixed, how might childcare costs shape parents’ work, birth decisions, and children’s opportunities?

selected.title: What could a million-gigabit cable change about the internet?
selected.summary: A report published October 17 describes a planned 4,300-mile subsea cable designed to carry data at a reported capacity of one million gigabits per second. The project illustrates how internet infrastructure increasingly depends on cables laid across the ocean floor.
selected.why_it_matters: More undersea capacity could affect cloud services, AI workloads, and the resilience of international data links, while leaving deployment and redundancy questions.
selected.challenge_question: Where will the reported 4,300-mile internet cable run?
selected.answer_explanation: The report describes a planned 4,300-mile subsea cable crossing the Atlantic. Its stated capacity is a project specification, not a measure of traffic already carried.
selected.butterfly_question: As more data travels through undersea cables, how might a failure or new route affect cloud services, AI, and everyday connectivity?

selected.title: Which kind of help do parents want most when babies are young?
selected.summary: A University of Michigan poll published October 19 found parents’ strongest support among listed programs was for paid leave during pregnancy or the newborn period, followed by food or formula assistance and childcare support.
selected.why_it_matters: The poll connects family budgets, work, and early-childhood policy, showing how support preferences can differ across specific programs.
selected.challenge_question: Which program had the strongest support among parents in the Michigan poll?
selected.answer_explanation: The poll found 73% strongly supported paid leave during pregnancy or the newborn period, ahead of food or formula assistance (60%), reduced-cost childcare (56%), car seats (55%), and diapers (51%).
selected.butterfly_question: If parents favor different kinds of help, how might policy choices affect who can keep working, afford care, and support a child’s early development?

selected.title: Are Mars’s moons captured asteroids—or debris from an ancient impact?
selected.summary: Ahead of the MMX launch, mission explainers note that Phobos and Deimos may be captured asteroids or remnants of an impact involving Mars. MMX plans to study the moons and return material from Phobos for analysis.
selected.why_it_matters: The moons’ origin could reveal how Mars evolved and clarify whether similar small bodies are captured or formed through collisions elsewhere in the Solar System.
selected.challenge_question: Which two leading ideas explain how Mars’s moons may have formed?
selected.answer_explanation: NASA and ESA describe two main possibilities: the moons could be asteroids captured by Mars’s gravity, or material left by a major impact on Mars. MMX’s observations and planned Phobos sample may help distinguish these hypotheses; they have not yet settled the question.
selected.butterfly_question: What could the answer to a moon’s origin story tell us about how planets gain moons—and where to search for habitable environments?
